archetype.name: Game Manager (quick-game)
archetype.definition: A veteran distributor who lives on short and intermediate throws to his tight end and possession receivers, keeps sacks down by getting the ball out, and rarely creates downfield.

report.headline: Efficient underneath, broken deep, and now losing his left tackle before a shootout.
report.take:
Brissett is who he has been for a decade: a big, sturdy pocket passer with a modest throwing profile who keeps an offense on schedule rather than stretching it. His intended air yards sit at 6.55, and he throws short of the sticks by almost two yards on average. That matches a career aDOT that has lived between 7.1 and 9.1. What is new in 2026 is the tempo. His time to throw has dropped to 2.6 seconds from 2.94 last year, and his pressure-to-sack rate has fallen from 28.5% to 18.5%, seventh-best among qualifiers. Arizona has built a quicker, tidier version of him.

The passing game splits cleanly by depth. On throws of 0-9 yards he completes 77% with positive EPA, and on the 27 intermediate attempts he has been genuinely good (+0.442 EPA, 59% success). Two zones drag the totals down. The first is the 26 throws behind the line, which are screens and swings that have lost real value. The second is the 11 deep shots: two completions, two interceptions. That is why a 67.8% completion rate comes with a 5.38 YPA that ranks 39th of 42. All six touchdowns have come in the red zone. He has not produced a single explosive scoring play.

Some of the line is flattered. Fifty of his 162 dropbacks came while trailing by nine or more, and there he has been excellent (+0.221 EPA, 78.7% completions) against defenses playing soft. In one-score games he is at -0.158. In close fourth quarters it is -0.902 on 18 plays, and on third down he converts just 31%. Week 4's three interceptions came with an aggressiveness rate of 45.7%, roughly triple his other games. That looks like a one-week departure from his style more than a new flaw, but it shows what happens when he is forced to push the ball.

The environment drives volume more than his skill does. Arizona's defense ranks 31st against the pass and 30th on deep throws, so the Cardinals are chasing points often. Weeks 3 and 4 both went well over the total. That keeps his attempts and fantasy floor healthy even when efficiency is mediocre. The new problem is that left tackle Paris Johnson Jr., a 100%-snap starter, is out for the season, and guard Isaiah Adams is questionable. The quick-release formula has been his protection plan, and it is about to be tested.

strengths.title: Short and intermediate accuracy
strengths.body: He wins in the 0-19 yard range, completing 77% short and turning intermediate throws into strongly positive plays. This is the core of how he has always played, and his CPOE has been positive in two of his last three seasons. It should hold as long as McBride stays the focal point.

strengths.title: Quicker clock, fewer sacks
strengths.body: His release time is down about a third of a second from last year, and his pressure-to-sack rate has dropped from 28.5% to 18.5%. This looks like a scheme-driven change toward quick game rather than luck, since his time to throw was similar in every game. It is the trait most at risk from the left tackle loss.

strengths.title: McBride as the safety valve
strengths.body: Trey McBride has drawn 46 targets at nearly +0.2 EPA per target, a reliable chain-mover for a QB who wants to throw short. Bourne has been productive on a small sample of 14 targets. The tight end connection gives Brissett a dependable read that does not require a clean pocket to hold up long.

concerns.title: No downfield game at all
concerns.body: He is 2 of 11 with two interceptions on throws of 20+ air yards. He has never been a deep passer, so this is mostly who he is, with some small-sample noise. The result is a ceiling problem: no long touchdowns and a YPA near the bottom of the league.

concerns.title: Garbage time inflates the line
concerns.body: His best numbers came trailing by nine or more, while one-score and late-close situations have been poor. Third-down failures, including a 31% conversion rate and four sacks, are where the quick game runs out of answers against tight coverage. This is a real limitation of the profile, not bad luck.

concerns.title: Left tackle gone for season
concerns.body: Paris Johnson Jr. played every snap before his biceps surgery, and Isaiah Adams is questionable with an ankle. Last year, behind less settled protection, Brissett took sacks on 28.5% of pressures. The quick release can mask some of this, but blind-side pressure is the likeliest way his sack and turnover numbers climb back.

trend.note: His games have alternated: +9 and +10 EPA passing games against the Chargers and 49ers, around a 95-yard dud against the third-ranked Seattle defense and a three-interception game against the Giants. The bad weeks came either against an elite defense or when he abandoned his usual low-risk style.

nextGame.headline: League-worst Lions defense sets up volume, but their rush bites
nextGame.body:
Detroit ranks dead last in defensive EPA, 30th against the pass and 32nd on deep throws. It allows 27.9 PPR points, 350 yards and 3.25 touchdowns a game to quarterbacks, all worst in the league. Its offense ranks fourth in pass EPA, and Arizona's pass defense is 31st, so this sets up as exactly the trailing, high-volume script where Brissett's numbers have piled up. The catch is that Detroit gets home: eighth in hit rate and sixth in sack rate. That is the one area where it can punish a line missing its left tackle.

Availability tilts toward Arizona's passing game on the back end. Detroit's secondary is thin: corner Rock Ya-Sin is doubtful, and safety Thomas Harper is on IR. Brian Branch is listed out and has not played this season, though his coach says he is close. On Arizona's side, Johnson is done for the year, while Adams, RB Jeremiyah Love and TE Hunter Long are all questionable. Losing Adams would put two new starters on the line against a good pass rush. Losing Love removes a back who has drawn 13 targets, though those have been inefficient ones.

keyMatchups.title: Lions rush vs. patched-up left side
keyMatchups.body: Detroit ranks sixth in sack rate and eighth in hit rate. Arizona is replacing an every-down left tackle and may be without Adams at guard. Whether Brissett's 2.6-second release survives this is the game's biggest question.

keyMatchups.title: Shootout script forces volume
keyMatchups.body: Detroit's pass offense ranks fourth in EPA, and Arizona's pass defense is 31st, so the Cardinals likely chase. He averaged 280 yards on 52 attempts in the Week 3 shootout with San Francisco. When trailing, he has been at his most efficient.

keyMatchups.title: A deep window he rarely uses
keyMatchups.body: Detroit is the worst deep-ball defense in the league and is short a corner and safeties. Brissett's deep game has been nonexistent, so the more realistic gain is intermediate throws to McBride and Bourne against a thin secondary.

nextGame.watch: How often Arizona keeps a tight end or back in to help on the left side, and whether his release time creeps above 2.6 seconds under Detroit's pressure.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume should hold. Arizona's defense is among the worst against the pass, which keeps the Cardinals throwing from behind and protects his yardage and fantasy floor. The efficiency he shows when trailing will not carry over to close games, and the third-down and late-game struggles reflect a limited downfield arm. Expect a season close to his 2025 profile: a few hundred yards of empty-calorie production, mid-pack EPA, and a TD rate tied to red-zone volume.

Two regressions pull in opposite directions. His interception rate should settle, since Week 4's forcing was out of character, and the deep-ball sample is only 11 throws. His sack avoidance is more likely to slip, because the line just lost its best pass protector. A YPA below 6 is plausible all year, given he throws short and has no consistent vertical threat other than occasional shots.
swingFactors: Pass protection without Paris Johnson Jr.
How often Arizona's defense forces shootouts
Whether Harrison Jr. becomes a real target over Wilson

bets.reason: Detroit allows a league-worst 350 yards a game to quarterbacks, and the 54.5 total points to a shootout in which Arizona likely trails. His 280-yard Week 3 came in exactly that kind of script.

Detroit gives up 3.25 touchdowns a game to the position, and all six of Brissett's scores have come on red-zone volume that a shootout should supply. His 53.6% red-zone completion rate tempers the edge.

Both defenses rank 30th or worse against the pass, Detroit's offense is sixth in EPA, and Arizona's last two games cleared their totals by 17.5 and 15.5 points. The number is high, so this is a lean, not a strong play.

confidence.note: Four games, volatile weekly results, and a season-ending left tackle injury that changes his protection.
